concepts.name: MCP tool annotations are untrusted hints

questions.prompt: On a Claude model that supports forced tool use, you send `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "get_weather"}`. Your user message also asks Claude to explain its reasoning before calling the tool. What comes back?

choices.text: A short text block with the explanation, then the `get_weather` call
A text-only answer if Claude judges the tool isn't needed this time
A 400 error, since a forced tool can't be mixed with prompt instructions
The `get_weather` call, with no natural-language text before it

questions.explanation: With `tool_choice` set to `any` or `tool`, the API prefills the assistant message to force a tool call, so Claude emits no natural-language text before the `tool_use` block, even when asked to. Option (a) is what you'd get with the default `auto` plus an instruction to use the tool. The request doesn't fail because of the instruction; forced tool use only errors where it's unsupported, such as with manual extended thinking or on models that reject it (Claude Opus 5.5 returns 400).

sources.title: Define tools (Claude API docs), section "Forcing tool use"
sources.claim: When `tool_choice` is `any` or `tool`, the API prefills the assistant message to force a tool call, so the model won't emit natural-language text before `tool_use` blocks, even if explicitly asked; to get an explanation plus a specific tool, use `auto` and ask for the tool in the user message.

questions.prompt: A third-party MCP server you don't control lists a `delete_records` tool annotated `readOnlyHint: true`. Per the MCP spec (revision 2026-07-28), how should your client treat that annotation?

choices.text: Trust it and auto-approve the calls, since the server says it has no side effects
As an untrusted hint: keep the user's confirmation step before each call
As invalid: reject the whole server, since annotations must be signed first
As a guarantee: the protocol layer blocks any write the hint rules out

questions.explanation: The spec says clients must consider tool annotations untrusted unless they come from trusted servers, and the schema calls every annotation a hint that may not describe the tool faithfully. So a third-party `readOnlyHint` can't justify auto-approval (a); keep a human in the loop who can deny the call. Nothing in MCP signs annotations, and the protocol can't enforce them, so (c) and (d) are wrong.

sources.title: Tools (MCP specification, revision 2026-07-28)
sources.claim: Clients MUST consider tool annotations untrusted unless they come from trusted servers; there SHOULD always be a human in the loop able to deny tool invocations, and clients SHOULD prompt for confirmation on sensitive operations.

sources.title: MCP schema.ts, revision 2026-07-28: ToolAnnotations
sources.claim: All ToolAnnotations properties are hints, not guaranteed to describe tool behaviour faithfully, and clients should never make tool use decisions based on annotations from untrusted servers.

questions.prompt: Your RAG system over many companies' quarterly reports retrieves the chunk "Revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter" for questions about the wrong company. Explain why plain chunking causes this and how Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval fixes it, including where the added context is used.

model_answer.summary: Chunking cuts a passage off from the document-level facts (which company, which quarter) that make it findable. Contextual Retrieval has an LLM write a short, chunk-specific context from the whole document and prepends it to each chunk before embedding it and before building the BM25 index.
key_points: Plain chunking loses context: the chunk alone doesn't say which company or period it refers to, so neither embeddings nor keyword search can match it to the right question.
An LLM is given the whole document and the chunk, and writes a short context (about 50–100 tokens) that situates the chunk in the document.
That context is prepended to the chunk for both the embedding (contextual embeddings) and the BM25 index (contextual BM25).
Adding a reranking step on top cut retrieval failures further than contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 alone.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's example is exactly this chunk: on its own it doesn't name the company or quarter. Contextual Retrieval prepends LLM-written context to each chunk before embedding and before BM25 indexing; in Anthropic's tests this cut top-20 retrieval failures by 49%, and adding reranking brought the cut to 67%. A common wrong answer is to add the context only to the embeddings, which leaves the BM25 index unable to match terms like the company name.

sources.title: Introducing Contextual Retrieval
sources.claim: Traditional chunking loses context (e.g. a chunk saying revenue grew 3% doesn't say which company or period); Contextual Retrieval prepends a 50–100 token chunk-specific context, written by Claude from the whole document, before embedding (contextual embeddings) and before creating the BM25 index (contextual BM25), cutting top-20 retrieval failures by 49%, and by 67% when reranking is added.

questions.prompt: Your app runs Claude with manual extended thinking (`thinking: {"type": "enabled"}`), must call `get_weather` for every weather question, and should show the user a one-line explanation first. Which `tool_choice` do you use, and why not `{"type": "tool", "name": "get_weather"}`?

model_answer.summary: Use the default `auto` and tell Claude in the user message to use `get_weather`. Forcing with `tool` fails with manual extended thinking and, where it works, prevents any text before the tool call.
key_points: With manual extended thinking, `tool_choice` of `any` or `tool` isn't supported and returns an error; only `auto` and `none` work.
Even where forcing is supported, `any` and `tool` prefill the assistant message, so Claude writes no natural-language text before the `tool_use` block.
`auto` plus an explicit instruction such as "Use the get_weather tool in your response" lets Claude explain and then call the tool.
`strict: true` on the tool definition can still guarantee schema-valid tool inputs without forcing the call.

questions.explanation: The docs list manual extended thinking as a setting where `any` and `tool` error, and recommend `auto` or `none` instead. They also say forced tool use prefills the assistant turn, so no explanation can come before the call. The tempting answer, `tool`, fails on both counts here; `auto` with a clear instruction in the user message gives both the explanation and the call.

sources.title: Define tools (Claude API docs), section "Forcing tool use"
sources.claim: With manual extended thinking (`thinking: {type: "enabled"}`), `tool_choice` `any` and `tool` are not supported and error, while `auto` and `none` work; `any` and `tool` prefill the assistant message so no text precedes `tool_use`; to get an explanation plus a specific tool, use `auto` and ask for the tool in the user message; strict tool use guarantees schema-valid inputs.

questions.prompt: An MCP server lists a tool with no `annotations` at all. Going by the `ToolAnnotations` defaults in the MCP spec (revision 2026-07-28), what should a client assume about the tool?

choices.text: It is read-only and safe to auto-approve, as no hint says anything otherwise
It makes only additive updates but may reach services on the open web
It may modify its environment destructively and reach external systems
It is idempotent, so the client can retry it freely after a timeout

questions.explanation: The defaults are the cautious ones: `readOnlyHint` false, `destructiveHint` true, `idempotentHint` false and `openWorldHint` true. So a tool with no annotations should be treated as one that may change things destructively, may not be safe to repeat, and may talk to the outside world. Assuming read-only (a) gets the default backwards, and even an explicit hint is only a hint unless the server is trusted.

sources.title: MCP schema.ts, revision 2026-07-28: ToolAnnotations
sources.claim: ToolAnnotations defaults: readOnlyHint false, destructiveHint true, idempotentHint false, openWorldHint true; all annotations are hints, and clients should never make tool use decisions based on annotations from untrusted servers.

questions.prompt: You add Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval to a hybrid RAG pipeline that uses both embeddings and BM25. Where does the short, LLM-written context for each chunk go?

choices.text: Prepended to each chunk before it is embedded and before BM25 indexing
Into the embedding input only, while BM25 indexes just the raw chunk text
Into chunk metadata, used only to filter results after vector search
Onto the user's query at search time, instead of onto stored chunks

questions.explanation: Contextual Retrieval prepends the chunk-specific context to the chunk text for both the embeddings (contextual embeddings) and the BM25 index (contextual BM25). Using both cut top-20 retrieval failures by 49% in Anthropic's tests, against 35% for contextual embeddings alone, so (b) leaves gains on the table. The context is generated per chunk at indexing time, not added to the query.

sources.title: Introducing Contextual Retrieval
sources.claim: Contextual Retrieval prepends chunk-specific explanatory context to each chunk before embedding and before creating the BM25 index; contextual embeddings alone cut top-20 retrieval failures by 35%, and contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 by 49%.

questions.prompt: Your RAG system over many companies' quarterly reports retrieves the chunk "Revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter" for questions about the wrong company. Which statements about Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The added context goes into the embeddings only, since BM25 can't use the extra words
The chunk alone doesn't say which company or quarter it is about, so search misses it
An LLM shown the whole document writes about 50–100 tokens of context for each chunk
The context is written at query time from the user's question, not when indexing
Adding a reranking step cut retrieval failures further than the contextual indexes

questions.explanation: Plain chunking loses context: the chunk doesn't say which company or period it describes, so neither embeddings nor keyword search can tie it to the right question. Contextual Retrieval has Claude read the whole document and write a short, chunk-specific context (usually 50–100 tokens) during preprocessing, and prepends it to the chunk before embedding (contextual embeddings) and before building the BM25 index (contextual BM25). Together they cut top-20 retrieval failures by 49%, and adding reranking took that to 67%.

sources.title: Introducing Contextual Retrieval
sources.claim: Traditional chunking loses context (a chunk saying revenue grew 3% doesn't say which company or period); during preprocessing Claude is given the whole document and the chunk and writes a 50–100 token chunk-specific context, which is prepended before embedding and before creating the BM25 index; contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 cut retrieval failures by 49%, and adding reranking by 67%.

questions.prompt: Your app runs Claude with manual extended thinking (`thinking: {"type": "enabled"}`), must call `get_weather` for weather questions, and should show a one-line explanation first. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: With manual extended thinking, `tool_choice` `any` or `tool` is unsupported and errors
`any` and `tool` prefill the assistant turn, so no text comes before the `tool_use`
Use `auto` and ask for the tool in the user message, so Claude explains, then calls it
`{"type": "tool", "name": "get_weather"}` still lets Claude write a short note first
`tool_choice` `none` forces a tool call but lets Claude write text before the call

questions.explanation: With manual extended thinking, forcing a tool with `any` or `tool` isn't supported and returns an error; only `auto` and `none` work, and `none` prevents tool use altogether. Even where forcing works, `any` and `tool` prefill the assistant message, so Claude writes no text before the `tool_use` block, even if asked. To get an explanation and then the call, use `auto` and say in the user message to use `get_weather`.

sources.title: Define tools (Claude API docs), section "Forcing tool use"
sources.claim: With manual extended thinking (`thinking: {type: "enabled"}`), `tool_choice` `any` and `tool` are not supported and result in an error, while `auto` and `none` work; `none` prevents Claude from using any tools; with `any` or `tool` the API prefills the assistant message, so the model emits no natural-language text before `tool_use` blocks; to get an explanation plus a specific tool, use `auto` and add explicit instructions in a user message.
